chapters.title: Chapter 1: Why Optimization Theory Matters for Portfolio Construction

lessons.title: Case Study: Framing the Minimum Variance Portfolio as an Optimization Problem

children.text: Before the next interview round, Ananya gets a take-home assignment by email. Build the minimum variance portfolio using these five Nifty 50 stocks, fully invested, no short-selling. Frame the problem properly before you touch a solver. She still cannot solve it by hand, that machinery arrives over the next five chapters, but Chapter 1 has given her everything she needs to frame it correctly. This lesson walks through that framing, step by step, on a slightly bigger and messier problem than the three-stock examples so far.

body.text: Correctly framing an optimization problem, choosing the right decision variables, the right objective, and every constraint that actually applies, is half the work. Get the framing wrong and no amount of sophisticated computation afterward answers the right question.

children.text: Five stocks across three sectors, deliberately chosen so two pairs sit in the same sector and one sits alone, mirroring how a real desk's shortlist rarely spreads evenly.

Five stocks, so five weights: w1 for HDFC Bank, w2 for ICICI Bank, w3 for TCS, w4 for Infosys, w5 for Hindustan Unilever. Nothing else in this problem is a decision variable. Expected returns and volatilities are inputs estimated from data, not choices.
This is a minimum variance portfolio, so the objective is unchanged in form from the last three lessons, only the size of the covariance matrix grows from 3x3 to 5x5.

body.caption: Minimize portfolio variance, now for five assets instead of three.
Illustrative annualized covariance matrix, rounded to 4 decimals. Note the high covariances between the two banking stocks (0.0546) and the two IT stocks (0.0420), reflecting shared sector risk.

markDefs.definition: A constraint requiring every portfolio weight to be zero or positive, ruling out short-selling. Combined with a budget constraint summing to 1, it restricts every weight to lie between 0 and 1.

children.text: Two rules apply here, one of each type from the last lesson. Full investment is the familiar equality constraint. No short-selling is a
, an inequality, applied separately to each of the five weights.

body.caption: Five inequality constraints: no short-selling, one per stock.

children.text: The objective is quadratic, the constraints are linear, so this is a quadratic program, same as every problem so far. But look closely at the constraint mix: one equality constraint and five inequality constraints together. Every problem in Chapter 1's earlier lessons carried equality constraints only.

body.text: This matters more than it looks. Lagrange multipliers, built in Chapter 4, are designed for equality constraints. They do not directly handle a rule like wi ≥ 0, because an inequality does not pin decision variables to a fixed curve the way an equality does, it only rules out one side of it. This five-stock problem is the first one in this course that genuinely needs the extended method, KKT conditions, covered in Chapter 5, which handle exactly this mix of equality and inequality constraints together.

markDefs.definition: The geometric shape formed by every point whose coordinates are all non-negative and sum to 1. It is the feasible region for any fully-invested, long-only portfolio.

children.text: Every combination of five non-negative weights summing to exactly 1 traces out a well-known shape in mathematics, called the

. Every fully-invested, long-only portfolio you will ever construct lives somewhere on this shape. It is bounded (no weight can run off to infinity) and it is convex, a property Chapter 2 defines precisely and shows is exactly why this problem, despite its five variables and six constraints, is guaranteed to have a solution that can actually be found.

body.title: Frame a bigger problem yourself
body.scenario: A different interviewer at another desk gives Ananya a new assignment: build the minimum variance portfolio from 7 Nifty 50 stocks, fully invested, no short-selling, with an added rule that no single sector's combined weight can exceed 50%.
body.prompt: Apply the same 5-step framing process. What are the decision variables? Write the objective, then list every constraint, noting which are equality and which are inequality.
body.modelAnswer: Decision variables: w1 through w7, one weight per stock. Objective: minimize wᵀΣw. Constraints: (1) w1 + w2 + ... + w7 = 1, an equality constraint, the budget rule. (2) wi ≥ 0 for every i, five to seven inequality constraints, no short-selling. (3) For each sector, the sum of the weights of stocks in that sector ≤ 0.50, an inequality constraint, the new sector cap. This problem has 1 equality constraint and multiple inequality constraints, so it needs the same KKT machinery from Chapter 5 that the no-short-selling rule alone already required.

body.title: Classify the new rule
body.question: The assignment is changed to also require exactly 40% of the portfolio held in banking stocks combined (HDFC Bank weight plus ICICI Bank weight equals 0.40). What type of constraint is this?
options: Inequality constraint, because it involves two stocks
Equality constraint, because it must be satisfied exactly
Not a real constraint, since it only affects two of the five weights
An objective function, not a constraint
body.explanation: The rule uses an equals sign and must be satisfied exactly. That makes it an equality constraint, just like the budget rule, except it restricts a subset of the weights (a sector total) rather than all of them individually.

body.label: Build your own covariance matrix on real data
body.description: Pull historical price data for actual Nifty 50 stocks and practice this 5-step framing process with real returns and volatilities instead of the illustrative ones used here.

points: Correctly framing an optimization problem, decision variables, objective, and every constraint, is half the work. Getting the framing wrong means no later computation answers the right question.
The 5-step framing process: identify the decision variables, write the objective function, write every constraint, classify the problem, and sanity-check the feasible region.
Real portfolio problems almost always mix equality constraints (budget, target return) with inequality constraints (no short-selling, position caps, sector caps).
That mix is exactly why this course builds Lagrange multipliers for the equality-only case first (Chapter 4), then extends to KKT conditions for problems with inequality constraints too (Chapter 5).

The feasible region for a fully-invested, long-only portfolio is a well-known convex shape called the probability simplex. Chapter 2 explains why that convexity guarantees a solution can be found at all.
